title: What are the best AI tools for keeping up with earnings?
summary: The best AI tools for keeping up with earnings on the stocks you own, with prices, AI summaries and alerts compared.
body_markdown:
## Which AI earnings tools are worth using?


### Seeking Alpha: best for AI summaries plus investor commentary


Seeking Alpha’s Earnings Call Insights are AI-generated summaries of earnings call transcripts, and they come with Premium. Premium also lets you link your brokerage accounts through Plaid and SnapTrade, so your portfolio updates daily on its own. You can get alerts by email or push, plus a daily email digest of news for each portfolio. Contributors also publish their own analysis, so you can read several takes on the same quarter.


Seeking Alpha says it isn’t a registered investment adviser. Premium costs $299 a year on its site, and its App Store listing also offers a $49 monthly plan.


### Quartr: best for listening to calls and reading the source


Quartr collects investor-relations material in one place, including live and recorded call audio, transcripts and slides. The mobile app is free, and it alerts you when an earnings call for a company you follow goes live. It’s a good place to check what management actually said before you trust a summary.


Its AI Summaries pull out revenue, margins and guidance, and they come with the desktop Pro plan, which is priced through sales. Quartr doesn’t connect to a brokerage, so you follow the companies yourself.


### Koyfin: best for earnings alongside charts and financial data


Koyfin’s transcript summaries pick out KPIs, segment commentary, guidance, risks and highlights from the Q&A, with unlimited use on every paid plan. Its alerts cover press releases, news, earnings transcripts and filings across your watchlists or portfolios, by desktop notification, email or push. You get 5 alerts on the free plan, 50 on Plus and 500 on Premium.


Plus starts at $39 a month and Premium at $79 a month, with higher rates if you pay month to month. For individuals, Koyfin doesn’t link brokerage accounts, so holdings are entered by hand. It suits investors who already do their research in charts and stock screeners.


### Yahoo Finance: best as a free starting point


On Yahoo Finance’s earnings call pages, a short AI summary of the results, guidance and cautions sits next to a full transcript provided by Quartr. You can link a brokerage account to track your holdings, and push alerts cover news, events and big price changes for the symbols you follow.


Yahoo says it isn’t a broker-dealer or investment adviser. The basic service is free, and paid plans start at $7.95 a month billed yearly.


### Perplexity Finance: best for asking questions about a report


Each company’s earnings page on Perplexity shows the results against estimates and a written set of highlights covering segments, margins and next-quarter guidance, with transcripts and audio from Quartr. Perplexity has also announced a calendar view and live summaries of calls in progress. You can ask follow-up questions in plain language, and on desktop you can connect your accounts through Plaid.


Its alerts are price alerts by email or push rather than earnings alerts. Perplexity has a free plan, and Pro and Max cost $17 and $167 a month billed yearly. Perplexity says its finance pages aren’t meant as investment advice.


### Robinhood: best for Robinhood customers


If your stocks are at Robinhood, you already get earnings notifications for what you own, and its Earnings Hub plays calls live with a transcript. Robinhood Gold members also get Digests, plain-language summaries of what may move their holdings, including upcoming events like earnings.


Robinhood says Digests aren’t investment advice. Gold costs $5 a month after a 30-day trial, it only covers your Robinhood accounts and Digests aren’t available for IRAs.


### Astor: our top pick for earnings on the stocks you own


Astor connects to the brokerage, retirement and crypto accounts you already have at most major US institutions, like Robinhood, Schwab and Coinbase, and follows every position you own along with the earnings dates, filings and headlines that touch them. On Pro and Max, when a report crosses a line you care about, it texts you what happened, why it matters to your portfolio and what you could do, and it stays quiet when nothing matters.


You can set a[scheduled alert](https://www.astor.app/blog/scheduled-alerts) for the day before a company you own reports, and Astor can schedule its own check-in after the results come out.[At a glance](https://www.astor.app/blog/at-a-glance) gives you a brief before the open and a recap after the close. You can also[text Astor](https://www.astor.app/blog/talk-to-astor-in-imessage) a follow-up about what changed, and it answers with live prices, news and filings.


Astor is an SEC-registered investment adviser, so its recommendations are personalized investment advice, and you make every decision. It’s free to start, and the free plan includes one custom alert. There’s no Android or web app and it’s US only. It also isn’t a transcript library or a way to listen to calls. The AI can be wrong, which is why every alert links to its reasoning and sources and you make the call.
